subject: Copywriting
title: Think Small: The VW Revolution
description: One-minute skill: Think Small: The VW Revolution.

hook.text: In 1960, every car ad boasted about size and power. Then Volkswagen ran an ad with two words: 'Think Small.'

buildup.text: Doyle Dane Bernbach broke the rules: honest copy, self-deprecating humor, massive white space, tiny car photo.

discovery.text: Americans loved big cars. The ad didn't fight that—it made smallness a virtue. Contrarian positioning worked.

twist.text: VW was a German car in post-WWII America. The ad had to overcome not just size bias but wartime associations.

climax.text: Ad Age named 'Think Small' the #1 ad campaign of the 20th century. Two words redefined advertising.

punchline.text: Two words. #1 ad of the century. Less is more.

quiz.question: Which agency created the 'Think Small' ad?

details.summary: Volkswagen's 'Think Small' campaign by DDB in 1959 broke every rule of automotive advertising. While competitors boasted about size and luxury, VW celebrated being small, ugly, and economical. The self-deprecating honesty revolutionized advertising and launched the Creative Revolution.
details.whyItMatters: Think Small proved that honesty and self-awareness could be more persuasive than exaggeration. It changed advertising by treating consumers as intelligent adults who appreciated candor.
takeaways: The campaign broke rules by celebrating the car's small size
Self-deprecating honesty was more persuasive than competitor boasting
Think Small is often ranked the greatest print ad campaign of all time

faq.question: Why was 'Think Small' considered revolutionary?
faq.answer: In 1959, American car ads featured huge cars, chrome, and boastful claims. VW's ad showed a tiny car surrounded by white space with self-deprecating copy. It acknowledged the car's limitations and turned them into advantages — a radical departure that treated readers as intelligent.

faq.question: How did Think Small change the advertising industry?
faq.answer: It proved that wit, honesty, and minimalism could sell products as effectively as spectacle. It launched the Creative Revolution of the 1960s, inspiring a generation of copywriters to reject formulaic advertising in favor of bold, intelligent communication.
